title: Prevention for tomorrow?
author: John Wills Lloyd
summary: John Wills Lloyd begins with early-2000s Ad Council public service ads on learning differences and links them to today's renewed concern, signalled by Sold a Story, about not letting children fail at basic academic skills. He recalls a Marilyn Jager Adams video that explains how a child who watches classmates learn to read while he does not concludes that he is stupid and that school is stupid. Lloyd argues children do not have to think that, because instruction can be designed so they conclude they are capable, which is the core promise of response to instruction and multi-tiered systems of support. The catch is that some methods are more effective than others, and he recommends using documented methods even when they do not match educators' gut instincts. He is indifferent to the diagnostic label, since educators are obliged to teach any child effectively by setting a goal, determining what must be known, applying evidence-based procedures and monitoring whether they work.
points: Early reading failure teaches children a damaging story about themselves that effective first instruction can prevent.
Response to instruction and multi-tiered systems of support rest on a simple principle: give students effective instruction in the first place.
Documented methods should outrank gut instinct when choosing how to teach.
Diagnostic labels matter less than the duty to teach effectively and to monitor whether instruction works.
quotes: We are experiencing, in my view, a resurgence of concern about not letting kids fail in acquiring fundamental academic competencies (viz, Sold a Story).

Kids start school, and they think that reason they are at school is to learn stuff, especially reading. This is their first chance out in the big world. But, the child who watches his peers succeed and recognizes that he is not getting it thinks, “I can’t do it. I’m stupid. Reading is stupid. School is stupid.

We do not need kids to think that. And they do not have to think it. They can think that they are smart, as the actors in the foregoing ad spot say. Just as the preschoolers demonstrate in the antique videos of Zig Engelmann challenging them to solve equations with missing addends show. Educators can provide instruction that obviates the “I’m stupid” conclusion. Kids can achieve. Indeed, that is an important idea associated with currently popular “response to instruction” and “multi-tiered systems of support”: Give students effective instruction in the first place.
We are back to effective instruction. And, we know that some methods of instruction are more effective than others.

So, should we employ instructional methods, practices, procedures, and curricula that have been documented to be effective? I think so. I recommend that educators do so, even though those effective methods may not appeal to their gut instincts.

The key idea, in my view, is that we know how to teach kids so that they don’t get the idea that there is something the matter with them. They can learn and they can learn that they are capable and competent.
Educators can provide instruction that obviates the “I’m stupid” conclusion. Kids can achieve.
